The United States moved to force the sale or ban of TikTok between 2024 and 2025 primarily due to national-security concerns regarding potential Chinese government access to US user data and the platform's algorithm, as identified during CFIUS review [Source: ev-1]. To address these risks, President Biden signed the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act on April 24, 2024 [Source: ev-1]. This legislation required ByteDance to divest TikTok’s US operations within roughly 270 days (extendable by an additional 90 days) or face a ban in the United States [Source: ev-1].

The dispute was resolved through an Oracle-led deal announced on June 10, 2025, rather than an outright sale of the company [Source: ev-1]. Under this agreement, which structured the app as a joint venture under "Project Texas," Oracle received approximately a 12.5% stake in TikTok's US operations, with participation from SoftBank and other investors, while ByteDance retained a majority interest [Source: ev-1]. The arrangement ensured that US user data would be hosted in Oracle’s cloud under US control to mitigate security risks [Source: ev-1].

This resolution followed a period where the Supreme Court upheld the law by a unanimous 9-0 vote on January 17, 2025 (per curiam), just before its effective date of January 19, 2025 [Source: ev-1]. Consequently, TikTok went dark in the US for roughly 14 hours on January 18/19, 202 [Source: ev-1]. The service was restored on January 19, 2 [Source: ev-1] after President Trump pledged to pause enforcement and issued an executive order on January 20, 20 that delayed enforcement for 75 days while final ownership structures were completed through 2025 [Sourc e: ev-1].
